# Valve Clearance Specifications for the 2006 Honda Fit 1.3L (L31A)

Adjusting valve clearances on a second-hand vehicle without the original service manual is a classic mechanical puzzle. The frustration of conflicting online data is real, but for the L31A engine found in the 2006 Honda Fit (Jazz), the specifications are well-documented in OEM repair manuals rather than scattered across unreliable forums.

For the L31A 1.3L i-DSI DOHC engine, the cold valve clearance measurements are precise: **0.15 mm for intake valves** and **0.25 mm for exhaust valves**. These tolerances apply specifically when the engine is at operating temperature of roughly 80Â°C to 90Â°C, but most mechanics perform this adjustment on a cold engine to ensure consistency with the "cold" spec found in literature. If you are using a feeler gauge, remember that thermal expansion will alter these readings slightly once the engine heats up; however, adhering to the manufacturer's cold specification is the standard industry practice for this powertrain.

## Why the Distinction Matters

It is tempting to treat all valves equally, but the difference between 0.15 mm and 0.25 mm is not arbitrary. The exhaust valve operates in a significantly harsher environment. It endures higher thermal loads and rapid temperature cycling during combustion cycles. This causes the exhaust valve stem to expand more than the intake valve when hot.

If you were to use the intake clearance of 0.15 mm for the exhaust valve, you risk the valve not seating properly once the engine reaches operating temperature. A gap that is too tight on the exhaust side leads to burning valve tips, loss of compression, and eventually a melted exhaust valve. Conversely, setting the intake valves to 0.25 mm would create excessive noise during operation without providing any meaningful benefit to combustion efficiency or longevity.

## The Adjustment Process and Tools

When approaching this task, the choice of tools dictates the accuracy of your results. While digital calipers are excellent for measuring parts, they are not the tool for setting valve lash on a running engine cycle. A high-quality set of feeler gauges is essential. For the L31A, ensure your gauge includes 0.15 mm and 0.25 mm blades with minimal tolerance variance (typically Â±0.01 mm or better).

The procedure involves rotating the crankshaft to position each cylinder at Top Dead Center (TDC) on the compression stroke. This is usually done using a T10 Torx socket on the harmonic balancer bolt or by aligning the timing marks on the cam cover. Once the rocker arm for the target valve is accessible, remove the cover and rotate the shaft until you feel slight resistance on the rocker arm.

Insert your 0.15 mm gauge into the intake rocker arm gap and the 0.25 mm gauge into the exhaust rocker arm gap. If the gauge slides in too easily or does not fit at all, adjust the clearance by turning the adjusting screw with a T20 Torx driver until you achieve the specified drag on the feeler blade. Tighten the lock nut while maintaining this drag to prevent the screw from loosening under vibration.

## Common Pitfalls and Trade-offs

A frequent mistake when adjusting valve clearances is ignoring the condition of the rocker arm shafts. On many L31A engines, the upper bearing surface of the rocker arms can wear down, creating play in the shaft itself. If you adjust to spec but the shaft has significant lateral movement, the effective clearance will fluctuate as the engine vibrates. Always check for shaft play before adjusting; if excessive play is detected, replacing the rocker arm assembly or the shaft bearings is a necessary prerequisite to achieving stable valve lash.

Another consideration is the type of lubrication used during adjustment. Applying oil to the feeler gauge can create a false sense of a tighter gap because the oil fills microscopic voids in the clearance. Wipe the area clean and ensure dry metal-to-metal contact with your gauge before making final adjustments. This ensures you aren't compensating for surface tension or oil viscosity when setting the mechanical limit.

If you encounter resistance that feels like it requires excessive torque to tighten the lock nut, stop immediately. The valve guide may be worn, or the cam lobe could be damaged. Forcing a fit here can lead to premature failure of the valve train components. In such cases, further disassembly for inspection is required before attempting another adjustment cycle.
